nodes.description: With RD3 absent, calcium-free GCAP1 and GCAP2 activate the residual RetGC in the inner segment, a compartment where the cyclase should be silent. This is the main driver of the rapid photoreceptor death: deleting GCAPs preserves most rd3 photoreceptors, and RD3 fragments that still inhibit the cyclase but cannot traffic it prevent degeneration without restoring function. Whether the toxicity comes from the misplaced cyclase activity itself or from a cyclase-independent action of calcium-free GCAPs is not settled.

nodes.description: RD3 binds RetGC1 and RetGC2 in the inner segment and carries them out of the endoplasmic reticulum toward the outer segment. Without RD3 the cyclases are not exported from the endoplasmic reticulum, are not stably expressed, and are essentially absent from rod and cone outer segments. The C-terminal Arg158-Ser170 region of RD3 is required for this trafficking step but not for cyclase inhibition, which is why trafficking and degeneration can be separated experimentally.

nodes.description: RD3 is a high-affinity, noncompetitive inhibitor of RetGC1 and RetGC2 that opposes their activation by GCAPs. Its alpha-helical core (N-terminal to Gly148) binds the cyclase through two surface clusters and keeps it inactive while it is in the inner segment, before the RetGC:GCAP complex forms in the outer segment. Truncated disease alleles lose this inhibition.

nodes.description: Biallelic truncating RD3 variants (nonsense, frameshift and splice-site alleles, including the Mediterranean founder p.Arg38Ter) produce unstable, non-functional C-terminally truncated protein or none at all. RD3 is a 195-residue four-helix-bundle protein expressed in rods and cones; it binds RetGC1 and RetGC2 through a central helical interface and needs its C-terminal region to couple the cyclase to intracellular trafficking.

nodes.description: Subretinal AAV delivery of RD3 to photoreceptors is the only disease-directed approach and has been tested only in mice. In two rd3 strains, AAV8(Y733F) carrying Rd3 under the rhodopsin kinase promoter moved guanylyl cyclase from the endoplasmic reticulum to rod and cone outer segments, kept photoreceptors alive for at least 7 months, and restored ERG responses. Transgenic RD3 expression in rods likewise restored cyclase levels and photoresponses. No human trial has been reported; care for patients is supportive.
